text:
**For a typical full-size fridge, plan on about 1,000 Wh for roughly half a day to a day, and 1,500-2,000 Wh for a full 24 hours.** The inverter also needs to handle the compressor's startup surge.

## The three numbers to check

1. **Running watts:** A typical fridge draws about 100-250 W while the compressor is on, so almost any 1,000 W-class station covers this ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
2. **Surge watts:** The compressor spikes at startup. Estimates run from about 1,000-1,200 W for a top-freezer to 2,400 W for large or older units ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)). Look for a surge rating of at least 1,300 W, and higher for a big or old fridge. A station with plenty of battery can still trip at startup if its surge rating is too low. Also choose a pure sine wave inverter.
3. **Watt-hours:** A fridge cycles on only about a third of the time. One energy-label example averages about 41 W, or roughly 1,000 Wh per day. Adding inverter losses and 20% headroom gives about 1,400 Wh per day ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

## Rough sizing

| Outage length | Battery to look for |
|---|---|
| Up to ~12-17 hours | ~1,000 Wh |
| 24 hours | ~1,400-2,000 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800 Wh or more |

Find your fridge's own number on its yellow EnergyGuide label: kWh per year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 = average watts. A large side-by-side with an ice maker can average about double the example above. Keeping the door shut helps a lot. You can also look up your model in the DOE's Refrigerator and Freezer Energy Rating Search Tool ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/)).

## Options that fit (prices vary, so check before buying)

- **About 1,000-1,150 Wh (most of a day):**
  - [BLUETTI AC180](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) has 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W output and 2,700 W peak, at roughly $399-699.
  - [Jackery Explorer 1000 v2](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) has about 1,070 Wh and runs a fridge about 17 hours in HomeGrid HQ's estimate ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- **About 2,000 Wh (a full day or more):**
  - [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) has 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W rated and 3,000 W peak output, at $699.99 after coupon.
  - [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) has 2,048 Wh and 2,400 W output, and it's expandable up to 8 kWh. It lists at $899, and the code AFF5OFF was tested at $44.95 off ([details](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l)). That link is an affiliate link, so Dealectric earns a commission.

If you might face multi-day outages, or want to run other things like a router or lights, go for a 2,000 Wh unit or an expandable one. If you tell me your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year and how long an outage you want to cover, I can narrow it to one pick.
